utterances.text: And they cause symptoms. In other words, the person is suffering in some respects. They cause symptoms. They cause dysphoria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain what dysphoria is?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: It means feeling bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all personality disorders cause dysphoria; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Most of them do eventually. Not all the time, but eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, people with severe personality disorders might not recognise that they are feeling bad, would they?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: They might not for a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also stated in your direct examination that there was no crossing of the clusters. And then on cross-examination you said, oh, you didn't mean there was no crossing of the clusters. So, which one is it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, no, you were talking about Axis I versus Axis II. And, I mean, those are different axis; so, you know, there can be diagnosis in Axis I and Axis II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: In Axis II there is -- I'm not familiar with any crossing of the clusters. I mean, I suppose it's possible, but not in my experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And your experience mainly has been writing about PTSD with regards to Vietnam vets, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, my experience has just been with patients, evaluated patients, I've evaluated thousands of patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What articles have you ever written about personality disorders under DSM-IV?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: There was an article about paranoid personality. There was an article about paranoid personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: It's in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it within the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: It was an article in General Hospital Psychiatry. Let's see, 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in your direct examination you also stated that the accused refused to accept responsibility. Now, did you hear his testimony before the Court on Monday and Wednesday of this week?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Not on Wednesday. On Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear it on Monday?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're still claiming that he refuses to accept responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I'm saying that he avoids responsibility. Yes, I didn't hear anything -- I didn't hear anything that led me to believe that he accepts full responsibility. I mean, --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also, I believe, misstated the evidence in your direct examination. You stated that he claims that Delic ordered him to commit suicide. That isn't what he said, was it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: He said something about Delic in his taking of the pills, that Delic had something to do with that, either gave him the pills or was instrumental in that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he never said that Delic ordered him to commit suicide; did he?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I don't know if he said he ordered him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also made a blanket statement that Mr. Landzo blamed Delic for everything. Now, that's not --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: That's right, that was a blanket statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's not true?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also did state in your direct examination that Mr. Landzo is by no means anti-social, doesn't fit into that personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I don't believe he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that one of the other expert witnesses said let's not nit-pick. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: That was Dr. Gripon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He used the term nit-pick?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, he did. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also referred to being presented with the Defence submission on the definition of diminished mental responsibility under British Common Law; did you review that?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you reviewed the Defence submission on the proposal of the Defence of diminished mental responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, I saw something about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must have seen it so well you cited a 1960 case.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: That was from a book on practical issues in forensic -- it was a British book, I just happened upon it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your definition of abnormality of the mind was that a reasonable man would think that it was abnormal?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And didn't you say in your direct testimony that Mr. Landzo was by no means normal?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, he's not -- well, of course, what is normal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You as a reasonable person?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm saying Dr. Sparr is a reasonable person. I'm making that assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think he is a reasonable person.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Are you sure you want to make that assumption?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure there are people here that doubt that I'm a reasonable person at this point.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I'm sure there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think every one in his own estimation is a reasonable person.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I've been self-evaluating myself recently, and I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, going back to the questions.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I think he has a lot, I think he has a lot of conflicts within the spectrum that I described, you know. So whether that's normal or not normal, you know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your report that it's possible he was suffering from a form of depression in 1996, but possibility is not the norm that psychiatrists apply, is it? What is the norm?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, you know, since we're not there, you can't evaluate him in '96 because it's '98, so you have to take collateral information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I mean, I'm sure he was depressed, I mean, because he was having all kinds of symptoms of depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of collateral information, you never went to Bosnia, you never interviewed his friends or his family.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only collateral information you have are the --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Are the reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And what I was trying to say, the more accurate psychiatric term is not possibility, it's psychiatric probability; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I never -- probability, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true anything is possible?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But whether it's probable is more relevant.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you diagnosed Mr. Landzo, you said he was probably suffering from an acute stress reaction?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: PTSD and acute stress reaction are anxiety disorders, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, they are. That's very controversial, they are in the anxiety disorder grouping, but there's a lot of people that disagree with that and think they should be an effective disorder grouping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to look in your book right now --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I know, I know, I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It lists acute stress disorder right next to PTSD, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under the same disorder.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only difference is that the time relevant is different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you found absolutely no personality disorder in Mr. Landzo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that means that all the other three independent psychiatrists were in correct; right?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, I mean, I don't necessarily think that they are incorrect. I think that they were looking, I think some of them, I'm not talking about Dr. Gripon, but I think some of them were looking at him from more of a psycho-dynamic perspective. I don't think they were using DSM-IV, I think they were giving a psycho-dynamic formulation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of DSM-IV, that's not the international standard, is it? Are you aware of ICD-10?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I'm aware of it, but I don't use it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're not really familiar with international standards?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the nomenclature that they just may just not be American; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through your direct examination and cross-examination of Mr. Moran, you kept referring to Mr. Landzo as "people like this." Now, "people like this," are you describing personality traits, personality disorders --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Traits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. In your report, you say that he didn't have PTSD in 1992 because the symptoms were short-lived and only lasted within a month. Now, from standing here in July of 1998 and relating back to 1992, you can limit his response to PTSD within a four-week period? Is that what you said in your report?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: That's what I said in the report, but, I mean, it could have been longer than a month. I'm just not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it could really be a personality disorder that has instigated or started Mr. Landzo's flight into health. The person that you see today as hyper-adjusted, that could be a result of a personality disorder, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: It could be the result of personality traits. I don't think he has a personality disorder, but it could be the result of personality traits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to page 4 of your report, one, two, three, four, five, six lines from the bottom. You say in your report: "In fact, he basically meets none of the criteria that would reliably link" --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I know. You corrected me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: But to me, he still doesn't meet -- basically, he should meet all the criteria and he doesn't. He could meet some of them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there's no requirement that he meet all of the criteria, is there?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, actually, we don't have a requirement in that regard. I mean, the way this has been used is that people do meet all the criteria. That's the way we've used it so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's not what it requires under the criteria listed in DSM-IV, is it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: This isn't in DSM-IV. You're talking about the one that is linking PTSD to criminal behaviour?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The blank test, yes.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The idea is that they are supposed to meet all of them. In certain cases where this has been allowed, the individual in the case has met all the criteria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: By the way, what you have to ask yourself about this is, in each case where this has been applied, there's been one incident, one incident, but this was ongoing, systematic, incident after incident, and, to me, that throws the whole thing out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This blank test that is not referred to in Kaplan and Sadok, they --

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Kaplan and Sadok is not a forensic book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it also is based upon Vietnam war vets; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we don't have any other information before us as to whether all of the criteria had to be fulfilled. Some of the criteria, one of the criteria, that isn't before this Court, is it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, it isn't, but PTSD is PTSD, whether it's Vietnam or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm going to next. Did you read the article by Dr. Miroslav Gareta (phoen) from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, did you notice in the back he even cites that he based it on an article by Landy Sparr?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right. He cites me twice. It has to be a good article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: But you do have some further questions, don't you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry, Dr. Sparr, I really do. In that article, there's quite a difference noted here. The situation in the Balkans in 1991, '92, '93, '94, versus Vietnam, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was a different situation. Go ahead. Ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the Vietnam war is one where it was a remote conflict with people from another country going over and taking part in a conflict they really didn't have any personal stake in. Would that be kind of accurate? Would that be accurate, not kind of. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: They had a personal stake in serving their country.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. In their honour and integrity as a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the difference is the war in Croatia, the war in Bosnia, those were wars that came to the people who were fighting, to their backyard. Would that be more correct?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Dr. Gareta writes about the differences and how the PTSD is more relevant in this situation than it would be in a Vietnam situation, and he cites several articles on Vietnam, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, but I don't agree with that. I mean, I don't agree that it's more relevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't believe that there's a difference in the two?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, I actually don't. I mean, I don't believe there's a difference in the PTSD. I think actually, in many ways, the Vietnam vets had it worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I just have one question from the article then, whether you agree or do not agree, that Dr. Gareta says: "The basic feeling of insecurity and endangerment was related to a much wider circle of potential enemies than can be rationally recognised, at least to a certain degree in a regular war." The enemy was totally unidentifiable, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: But that's exactly what happened in Vietnam. In Vietnam, the vets didn't know who the enemy was. They didn't know. It could be anybody around them. They faced exactly the same situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying that the Vietnam war, the conditions that the soldiers from the United States faced in Vietnam are identical to the conditions and issues that the soldiers faced in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, in the actual conduct of the conflict, I mean, while they were over there, they felt constantly in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was only the soldiers that were in danger. It wasn't their life, their families, their homes, and their heritage that was being attacked, was it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, but when they came back to the United States, they continued to feel constantly in danger. Many of them live in bunkers in remote areas because they are afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that could possibly be more severely applied to someone who is being attacked on their own home front; right?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I don't see a lot of difference. I think it's the same -- you know, I mean, they come back to the United States, and there's Vietnamese all over the place, and they think some of them might be North Vietnamese. I mean, they don't know. They feel the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go on to another thing you talked about. You said that in Vietnam it was not uncommon for people in such a group as the Phoenix squadron to recruit people like this, referring to Mr. Landzo. You meant someone with a severe personality disorder, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No, I didn't, not at all. I meant people that are overcontrolled, that will take orders, not people that are loose cannons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in your report, you said you do support the opinions of the other doctors that Mr. Landzo has a personality structure that was, perhaps, susceptible to influence by others and a history of being a follower and subservient to authority?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only in nomenclature does this basically differentiate from the other opinions of the other psychiatrists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you cannot give Mr. Landzo a psychiatric diagnosis, and he doesn't fit any criteria for DSM-IV. That doesn't mean that he doesn't have a personality disorder, does it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: It means that he doesn't have a personality disorder, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't there another section there under DSM-IV which says, "Otherwise not specified"?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I don't like that because it's a waste basket, but, yeah, I know it's there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it does exist, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to the fact that you have in your report come to certain forensic conclusions, and I'd like to ask you about them. I think the first forensic conclusion you came to was whether or not he fully comprehended the nature of the criminal act he is accused of committing. What standard is that? Where did you come up with that standard?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Can you point to that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's on page 5 under, "If Mr. Landzo does not have PTSD," then it is the second line, first sentence, "Whether or not he can fully comprehend the nature of the criminal act"?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I think that's got to do with his intent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking where did this standard come from?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I don't know if there's any specific -- I mean, I'm not quoting anything, so I don't ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your own standard that you've come up with?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would ask also that Ms. McMurrey read the whole sentence which says: "While everyone appears to agree that Mr. Landzo is not insane, there has been speculation about whether or not he can fully comprehend the nature of the criminal act he is accused of committing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That still is the same question. Where did he come up with the standard of insanity?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to determine whether Mr. Landzo was insane in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that that doesn't seem to be an issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. It's not an issue. The second standard that you appear to have come up with is, "Did he exhibit sufficient premeditation or criminal intent in 1992?" Now, what standard is that?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I guess that's got to do with diminished responsibility and that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's no where mentioned in the diminished responsibility definition, is it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, actually, in some things that I have seen, it is, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that that you've seen?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, it's not a legal opinion or anything, but it's more a description of what diminished responsibility entails.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there's no mention in diminished responsibility case law or definition or standard that deals with premeditation, does it?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you have a third standard here that you've referred to called, "Whether or not he could control or understand the parameters of his behaviour in 1992." Where does that standard come from?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I'm not trying to cite standards here. I'm just trying to put this in plain English. I mean, that isn't my intent to cite standards. I'm just trying to write a report and make it comprehensible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what you're doing is you're forming an opinion for this court based on some legal standard that you're applying, and I'm just trying to find out which one it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to her arguing with the witness, and specifically he has already said he was not coming to legal conclusions.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: I mean, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel is free to challenge whatever opinion that has been expressed, because the theory and practice of expert opinion is that the opinions that are preferred is that of the expert, and the expert goes to some extent to justify those opinions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third standard that you've come up with is whether or not he could control or understand the parameters of his behaviour in 1992. Is that another one that you just have come up with to explain things in your layman's terms?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just have one second? Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you, Dr. Sparr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. McHenry:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, both Mr. Moran and Ms. McMurrey talked about various portions of your report. In one sentence, one relied on one part of the sentence, and the other one relied on another part of the sentence. I would just like to ask you: Has it been your opinion that Mr. Landzo has a history of being a follower and subservient to authority, however, he tends to dwell on his subservience and use it as an excuse for his behaviour and to ameliorate his conscience. Is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one simple one. Perhaps it might have arose from your testimony. Is it your opinion, as a summary of what you indicated here, that all you have found here is that there is no personality disorder in Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: DR. LANDY SPARR
utterances.text: Right, he doesn't meet the criteria for the end of the spectrum kind of personality disorder. You know, I don't know where he is on the spectrum, but he isn't all the way at the far end, which is what is required to make these diagnoses of personality disorder. Certainly he has personality traits that work against him and that have made it possible for him to do what he's alleged to have done and may also make it understandable, in my opinion. But I couldn't say specifically that he's personality disordered in the sense of how DSM-IV describes these disorders. For instance, he's dependent, but he's not extraordinarily dependent, which is what you have to be to meet the standard. He's rather obsessive and avoidant, but not at the end -- once again, not at the end of the spectrum. So he has these kind of traits that stop short of being a full disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Sparr. You will not be required further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Don't worry, Dr. Sparr, other people have tried to walk off with them too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, I think we have an application from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you're talking about my motion to reopen, we'll withdraw that. We think you have heard more than sufficient evidence on that area in retrospect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is the end of the Defence case. You have no other witnesses. This is the only witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We have no other witnesses that Your Honours will allow us to call I think is fair. Just for Your Honours' information, we did file, based on the ruling of Your Honour, that what we believed was rebuttal was not correctly rebuttal. We did file this morning a motion to reopen for the limited purposes as set forth in the motion. That has been filed, and we would hope that possibly early next week we can have a motions hearing, but I understand that Your Honours will not have had a chance to examine it or the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, this is the end of the Defence case. Perhaps if there are any rejoinders which are likely to be, because there are none, and for any other applications, I think we may be able to deal with it. I don't expect any rejoinder witnesses. This is clear. If any needs to be filed, it has to be filed at the latest on the 3rd of August. That's on Monday, leaving us at least whatever witnesses you do have. If it is necessary to call them, we will do so. If it is not because they have been covered by whatever we have heard, then I will determine that. Now, if it is then filed then, and perhaps on that same day, by 2.30 p.m., then we will deal with whatever evidence we're prepared to deal with. I think we'll make a formal schedule on this so that it will be clearer for counsel who want to -- so that they can carry on with any preparation for closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: At the latest by Tuesday, the 25th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There's one outstanding application where we've asked the Trial Chamber to amend that schedule. For some reason, I had the 26th in mind. We've asked the Trial Chamber to amend that schedule to allow us to file 72 hours after we're served with the Prosecutor's brief on the theory that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is for that of closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, the final -- so that if we have to file on the 25th, they serve us 72 hours in advance, or if they file on the 25th, we file 72 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On the 28th, three days. Yes, I think that is what we're trying to provide. So if, as we now say, the Prosecution files the arguments on the 25th of August, then the Defence will file their response on the 28th of August. So it still leaves us 72 hours of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, at least from my standpoint, that's perfectly acceptable and we thank the Trial Chamber very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we are agreeable and everybody will accept that. Now, I remember you suggested the questions of mitigation in your brief. I think if you really have any arguments in mitigation, there's nothing wrong in your including it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can say, we were under the impression that at some point we would be able to present actual evidence of mitigation and it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is always available. It's always there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only legal issue we would have as to mitigation would go -- the legal issue, as opposed to a factual thing, would go to, and I don't have the Statute in front of me, but there's a provision in the Statute having to do with the sentencing procedures in the former Yugoslavia and also some provisions in Protocol 2 of the Geneva Conventions that we would point the Trial Chamber to. If you want to see that now, that's fine, we can give it to you or we can wait and give you sentencing and punishment as an entire package. I think it might be easier for the Trial Chamber to keep apples over here for guilt and innocence, and then oranges over here for punishment. Whatever is most convenient for the Court, I'll be doing the same amount of work in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I was about to say, perhaps you might understand that it is not really out of place in any submissions, even if arguments with respect to mitigation are included, irrespective of the fact that you might also lead evidence on a factual basis to show why those arguments are being put forward. It's not unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I understand it, we'll be able to present factual basis letter and also exercise our right of allocution at some future date after the 31st of August, if we get to the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it gets to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask. For layman's term, just to explain, we're still just dealing with guilt and innocence up until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Until a conviction. Then after that, you can then suggest other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since you said that you will order that by the 3rd of August, the submissions be filed, should the OTP have filed any submissions, the Defence would like to have enough time to respond. So we would ask kindly, Your Honours, to request the OTP to make their submissions tomorrow so that we have enough time by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there must be some error. I said by the 25th of August. That is when submissions should be filed. For any further rejoinder evidence, it could be by the 3rd of August. That's Monday. That's quite different from making submissions on the case as a whole. But any person wishing to call other witnesses should do that by Monday, the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think possibly maybe there was a misunderstanding. Mrs. Residovic, with what I said to the Court as heard or translated by Mrs. Residovic, the Prosecution has already filed its submission this morning. So that will be available for you today. I'm sorry if I wasn't clear for Mrs. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is all we have for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, just one final thing. Just to confirm, the final arguments are scheduled for the 31st of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the final submissions. What I mean is closing arguments are scheduled for the 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to just make it clear. This, of course, is on the assumption that no new evidence be submitted. In this situation, because should that be the case, we would, of course, ask for sufficient time to be made available to us to carry out the investigation and submit the fresh evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, we are not expecting any further evidence between now and these dates. What might have been done is just to satisfy all the provisions, because all the evidence is in. As far as we're concerned, we don't expect anything new, as I said at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The final submission by the Prosecution will be filed by the 25th and the Defence, the 28th, within 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ladies and gentlemen. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 12.47 p.m. to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of August, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 24 25
